The Shape of the DPO Hyperparameter Landscape: What to Measure, How It Moves with Scale, and When Not to Transfer It

Hannan Mahadik David Salinas ELLIS Institute Tübingen ELLIS Institute Tübingen & Prior Labs Germany Germany hannan.mahadik@tue.ellis.eu david.salinas@tue.ellis.eu Jacek Golebiowski Aaron Klein distil labs ELLIS Institute Tübingen Germany Germany jacek@distillabs.ai aaron.klein@tue.ellis.eu
Abstract

Direct preference optimisation (DPO) is widely used for language model post-training, but its performance depends strongly on the choice of its hyperparameters, such as the learning rate and the reference-policy regularisation parameter β\beta. To better understand the DPO hyperparameter landscape, we conduct extensive experiments using a dense hyperparameter grid across different model scales from the same family. This allows us to analyse how the optimal DPO hyperparameters evolve with model size and the number of update steps, with intermediate checkpoints providing an inexpensive signal to accelerate the hyperparameter optimisation process. Furthermore, by evaluating our models on both static and dynamic benchmarks, we identify which benchmarks provide the strongest signal for hyperparameter selection. Finally, we investigate how different state-of-the-art hyperparameter optimisation strategies perform in this setting. Our experiments show that the optimal learning rate varies with model size and that hyperparameters are not transferable across training datasets. We also find that validation loss is a poor proxy for hyperparameter optimisation, as hyperparameters that minimize validation loss only weakly correlate with optimal hyperparameters for downstream benchmarks. Therefore, DPO hyperparameters need to be tuned specifically for the target model, dataset, and evaluation objective. We also show that short candidate training runs can substantially reduce the cost of this selection. We release all our training configurations and evaluation results to support reproducible analysis of selection quality and training cost.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly advanced in both capability and scale, but pretrained models are not necessarily well-suited for interaction with users: they may fail to reliably follow instructions, answer questions, or respond appropriately to user intent. Post-training is therefore a critical step in transforming a pretrained model into a useful assistant  (Ouyang et al., 2022). Common post-training recipes consist of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which teaches a model to follow instructions using demonstration data, followed by preference optimisation that adapts model behaviour toward preferred responses.

Direct preference optimisation (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) optimises directly from preference pairs relative to a fixed SFT reference policy, without a separate reward-model training stage. Its learning rate controls the size of the update, while β\beta controls the strength of the reference-adjusted preference signal in the DPO objective and therefore the objective’s trade-off between fitting preference pairs and remaining close to the reference policy. Both hyperparameters may therefore have effects that depend on the reference checkpoint and preference data. Prior work has already shown sensitivity to β\beta and the characteristics of preference pairs  (Wu et al., 2024). This raises the question: how reliably can a DPO configuration selected in one setting be applied to another?

Post-training recipes commonly report configurations that perform well for a particular model, dataset, and reference checkpoint, often using a fixed suite of static capability benchmarks to guide those choices (Tunstall et al., 2024; Ivison et al., 2023; Lambert et al., 2025; Team Olmo, 2025; Allal et al., 2025). These configurations are then generally reused across related models or experiments, implicitly assuming both that the configuration transfers and that the static evaluation signal used to select it remains informative. Whether either assumption holds across model scale has received substantially less systematic investigation. Getting this wrong is not a minor efficiency loss. In our primary sweep, the gap between the best and the worst configuration within a single model size reaches roughly 295 Elo points at a 4B parameter scale (Figure 1). Under the fitted Bradley–Terry model used to construct these scores, this corresponds to an estimated 84.5%84.5\% probability that the best configuration wins a pairwise comparison with the worst. By comparison, the DPO improvement over its SFT checkpoint is 176 Elo points, corresponding to a 73.3%73.3\% win probability. The worst configurations in the grid also land below the SFT checkpoint. A poor configuration can therefore erase the entire benefit of the stage and leave a model worse than its SFT checkpoint.

We study DPO selection across five Qwen3 (Qwen Team, 2025) sizes (0.6B–14B), three complementary Llama models (Grattafiori and others, 2024; Meta AI, 2024), eleven downstream benchmarks, and two LLM judges. Fully logged training trajectories allow us to analyse configuration transfer and compare single- and multi-fidelity hyperparameter optimisation (HPO) methods without additional training. We release the resulting checkpoint-level benchmark, representing approximately 11,849 H100 GPU-hours of completed DPO training and evaluation (including the complementary experiments), so future work can reuse these results without having to repeat this compute. Appendix C.1.1 provides the breakdown.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    Evaluation signals for DPO tuning. We show that validation loss is an unreliable selection signal and that chat benchmarks produce more consistent configuration rankings than static benchmarks, with limited sensitivity to the choice of the judge model used.

  • •

    Transfer across scale and training data. We show that DPO configurations do not reliably transfer across model sizes or training preference datasets. Preferred learning rates exhibit an overall decrease with Qwen3 model scale, but configuration rankings can vary sharply even between neighbouring models.

  • •

    Compute-efficient hyperparameter selection. Partial model training runs can provide useful ranking information within roughly 2020–30%30\% of training. We also show that under sufficient budgets, adaptive HPO methods can outperform random search.

  • •

    An offline benchmark for DPO hyperparameter selection. We release checkpoint-level Qwen3 and Llama trajectories with training costs and scores on eleven benchmarks, along with code to reconstruct the surrogate environments and HPO experiments. This enables reproducible research on selection signals, early-selection policies, transfer, and compute allocation without repeating these expensive DPO runs.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 situates our study within work on DPO, hyperparameter transfer, and evaluation reliability. Section 3 describes the models, data, training grids, evaluation suite, downstream aggregation objectives, and offline HPO simulation framework. Section 4 presents the empirical results, followed by practical recommendations, limitations, and conclusions. The appendix provides complete experimental settings, supplementary analyses, and detailed HPO simulation results.

2 Related Work

DPO and hyperparameter sensitivity.

DPO optimises preferences relative to a fixed reference policy without training a separate reward model (Rafailov et al., 2023). Alternative objectives such as ORPO and SimPO change the treatment of the reference policy, preference margin, or regularisation (Hong et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2024). We hold the DPO objective fixed to isolate hyperparameter transfer within one method and leave an extension of this analysis with alternate preference-optimisation objectives to future work. Prior work shows that DPO is sensitive to training data (Ivison et al., 2024) and the joint choice of learning rate and β\beta (Wu et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2024), while post-training recipes tune these values for their particular models and datasets (Tunstall et al., 2024; Ivison et al., 2023; Lambert et al., 2025). We quantify how a jointly selected (learning​rate,β)(\mathrm{learning\ rate},\beta) configuration transfers across model scales and preference data, and whether the target model reveals a suitable configuration before training completes.

Hyperparameter transfer and scaling.

Scaling laws characterize how training behaviour changes with model and data size (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022), while μ\muTransfer and related work study when hyperparameters tuned on smaller models predict larger-model behaviour (Yang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2025a). DPO presents a different setting because it follows pretraining, depends on an SFT reference policy, and introduces preference-specific hyperparameters. We test whether an analogous learning-rate trend appears in DPO and assess whether configurations selected at one scale remain effective at another.

Evaluation signals and benchmark reliability.

Post-training studies commonly use both fixed capability benchmarks and LLM-as-judge evaluations such as MT-Bench  (Zheng et al., 2023), AlpacaEval  (Dubois et al., 2024), and Arena-Hard  (Li et al., 2025b). LLM-as-judge evaluations have documented sensitivities including position bias  (Wang et al., 2024), length bias  (Dubois et al., 2024), and model self-preference  (Panickssery et al., 2024). Relatedly, FineTasks selects multilingual evaluation tasks using properties such as non-random performance, low variability, and stable model rankings across training checkpoints (Kydlíček et al., 2024). Our setting is closely related but addresses a distinct post-training question: whether a metric provides a reliable ranking signal for hyperparameter selection. We examine whether validation loss, static capability benchmarks, and chat-based evaluations produce consistent rankings over DPO configurations, and whether rankings observed at intermediate checkpoints predict the final ordering of configurations. Evaluation is therefore treated not only as a reporting mechanism but as part of the HPO problem itself.

3 Experimental Setup

Models.

We select Qwen3 as the primary model family because it provides competitive, text-only base checkpoints at multiple practical scales (Qwen Team, 2025). Our study uses the 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B, and 14B models, which span a 23×23\times parameter range within one family. This allows us to study how DPO hyperparameter selection changes with size while holding the model family and modality fixed. Complementary experiments on Llama models are reported in Appendix D.2.

Data.

We first perform SFT on Dolci-Instruct-SFT and then train with DPO on Dolci-Instruct-DPO (Team Olmo, 2025). To isolate the effects of training data, we also repeat the shared DPO grid on UltraFeedback Binarized (Cui et al., 2024) dataset for the same Qwen3 models. For this ablation, we retain the SFT checkpoint and evaluation suite while replacing the DPO training dataset.

Training Protocol.

We use an SFT learning rate of 3×10−53\times 10^{-5} for all primary runs, while comparing DPO configurations across model sizes. Appendix C.2 reports a five-point SFT learning rate sweep showing that this learning rate choice lies in a stable regime. Rankings vary across the five sizes and evaluation aggregates, and the highest learning rate tested consistently degrades the downstream performance. We leave joint optimisation of the SFT and DPO hyperparameters to future work. DPO begins from the corresponding SFT checkpoint. Its search space contains a fully observed 3×33\times 3 core shared by every model: learning rates ∈{1×10−6, 2×10−6, 4×10−6}\in\{1\times 10^{-6},\,2\times 10^{-6},\,4\times 10^{-6}\} and β\beta values ∈{0.01, 0.02, 0.04}\in\{0.01,\,0.02,\,0.04\}. We extend this core where needed to cover each size’s promising learning-rate range. The shared core supports like-for-like transfer and the size-specific extensions inform the local optimum. We save intermediate checkpoints and evaluate them alongside the final checkpoints. All other training settings are held fixed within each sweep. Per-size search spaces, checkpoint steps, training settings, and distributed training setups are reported in Appendix C.3. All post-training runs use TRL  (von Werra et al., 2022).

Evaluation.

We evaluate eleven benchmarks in two groups. The chat group comprises Elo (Chiang et al., 2024), Arena-Hard (Li et al., 2025b), MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023), and length-controlled AlpacaEval 2.0 (Dubois et al., 2024). These evaluations measure instruction following and response quality through LLM judgments. We score the chat responses separately with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct and Gemma 4 31B-it (Qwen Team, 2025; Gemma Team, 2026) to assess their sensitivity to judge choice (Wang et al., 2024; Panickssery et al., 2024). The main paper results use the Qwen model as the judge, unless specified otherwise. The static group comprises ARC-C (Clark et al., 2018), GPQA (Rein et al., 2024), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022), and IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023). We select these benchmarks to cover distinct capabilities commonly examined in language-model evaluation: scientific and mathematical reasoning, commonsense and physical reasoning, truthfulness, and instruction and format compliance. This diversity allows us to test whether a configuration that performs well on one fixed capability transfers to other capabilities, and to monitor capability-specific regressions during DPO. We also record validation loss as a candidate selection signal. The static benchmarks use lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2023). The chat benchmarks use their corresponding benchmark implementations, including JudgeArena for MT-Bench and Elo ratings (Lushtaku et al., 2026), with candidate and judge models served through vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). Complete benchmark settings are reported in Appendix C.4.

Aggregation and Selection Criteria.

For configuration ii and benchmark bb, let xi,bx_{i,b} denote the observed benchmark score for a specific configuration. Because the scales across benchmarks differ, we standardize scores as zi,b=(xi,b−μb)/σbz_{i,b}=(x_{i,b}-\mu_{b})/\sigma_{b}, where μb\mu_{b} and σb\sigma_{b} are the mean and population standard deviation of benchmark bb across the relevant configuration pool. For an aggregate GG of benchmarks, we average these standardized scores as Zi,G=1|G|​∑b∈Gzi,bZ_{i,G}=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{b\in G}z_{i,b}. We use GG for the aggregation of chat benchmarks (ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}), static benchmarks (ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}}), or all benchmarks (ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}}). Trajectory plots use final-grid statistics as a fixed reference, whereas checkpoint-selection analyses recompute them at each step. For configuration ii and aggregate GG, we define normalised regret as Regreti,G=maxj∈𝒞⁡Zj,G−Zi,Gmaxj∈𝒞⁡Zj,G−minj∈𝒞⁡Zj,G\operatorname{Regret}_{i,G}=\frac{\max_{j\in\mathcal{C}}Z_{j,G}-Z_{i,G}}{\max_{j\in\mathcal{C}}Z_{j,G}-\min_{j\in\mathcal{C}}Z_{j,G}} where 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the set of jointly scored configurations used for the comparison: normally the full grid at one model size, and the shared 3×33\times 3 core at the target size for cross-scale transfer. Thus, regret is zero for the best configuration in 𝒞\mathcal{C} and one for the worst.

Offline HPO Simulation.

Hyperparameter optimisation (HPO) (Franceschi et al., 2025) uses the outcomes and costs of earlier trials to decide which training configurations to evaluate next. Multi-fidelity HPO additionally uses partial training runs as cheaper, lower-fidelity signals when allocating further compute. Training progress is the fidelity variable. Each method optimises ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} under matched budgets, and we evaluate its recommended configuration at true final fidelity. At each Qwen3 size, we fit four surrogate blackboxes separately: a Gaussian process (Williams and Rasmussen, 2006) and one-, three-, and five-nearest-neighbour regressors (Hastie et al., 2009). This offline-HPO setup enables repeated comparisons under matched budgets and random seeds, although its conclusions are conditional on the fitted interpolation models. We compare three single-fidelity methods, random search (Bergstra and Bengio, 2012), TPE (Bergstra et al., 2011), and CQR (Salinas et al., 2023), which evaluate every proposed configuration to completion, with the multi-fidelity methods ASHA (Li et al., 2020a) and BOHB (Falkner et al., 2018), which allocate compute using intermediate results from step 400 onward. Each setting uses two workers and 25 seeds under an 8×8\times wall-clock budget and a restrictive one-unit budget, corresponding to approximately two full-run equivalents of aggregate compute across both workers. At each cutoff, we evaluate the recommended configuration at final fidelity; before any trial completes, we compare candidates at their highest shared fidelity. The simulations use syne-tune (Salinas et al., 2022). Appendices A and C.5 give additional related work and full HPO settings.

4 Results

4.1 Identifying The Metric To Tune On

Validation loss is an unreliable selection criterion.

Validation loss is an insufficient proxy signal to select hyperparameters as it poorly correlates with downstream performance (see Figure 2). Selecting the configuration with minimum validation loss yields mean normalised regret of 0.500.50, 0.620.62, and 0.530.53 under ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}}, ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, and ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}}, respectively. At 0.6B, it selects the worst configuration under ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}. Pooled across sizes, rank correlations are only 0.100.10, 0.180.18, and 0.140.14, and sometimes change sign across scales. Because DPO loss depends on β\beta, we also rank learning rates separately within each fixed β\beta. Agreement with ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} still varies across Qwen3 sizes (ρ=−0.67\rho=-0.67 to 0.670.67; Appendix D.1.2). The underlying benchmark-level correlation matrices appear in Appendix D.1.1.

Chat benchmarks produce more consistent configuration rankings.

We measure the pairwise Spearman correlation between the configuration rankings produced by benchmarks within each evaluation group. Table 1 shows that mean agreement among static benchmarks is consistently weak across the five Qwen3 sizes, whereas mean agreement among chat benchmarks is consistently positive. Agreement also varies among benchmark pairs: the standard deviation ranges from σ=0.10\sigma=0.10 to 0.200.20 for chat-benchmark pairs, compared with σ=0.37\sigma=0.37 to 0.640.64 for static-benchmark pairs. Higher agreement does not establish that chat benchmarks measure ground-truth quality, but it indicates that hyperparameter selection based on the chat group is less sensitive to the particular benchmark chosen. Because the static suite intentionally spans heterogeneous capabilities, its lower agreement is partly expected and should not be interpreted as evidence that its individual benchmarks are invalid. Instead, the result shows that the DPO configuration preferred for one capability may not be preferred for another. The corresponding Llama and Qwen3 (UltraFeedback) analyses in Appendices D.2 and D.1.12 show the same pattern.

Static and chat aggregates favour different configurations.

At Qwen3-4B, maximizing ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}} selects (2×10−6,0.01)(2\times 10^{-6},0.01), whereas maximizing ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} selects (4×10−7,0.01)(4\times 10^{-7},0.01). Figure 3 shows that these configurations occupy different parts of the Pareto frontier. Thus, the appropriate learning rate depends on whether the intended target is static capability, chat quality, or an explicit aggregate of the two. Appendix D.1.5 provides the corresponding Pareto comparisons for the other four Qwen3 sizes.

Independent judges largely agree on chat-performance rankings.

To test sensitivity to judge choice, we compare the ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} configuration rankings produced independently by Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct and Gemma 4 31B-it over the nine-configuration learning-rate–β\beta core. Agreement is high for Qwen3-1.7B and larger models, with Spearman correlations of ρ=0.90\rho=0.90, 0.980.98, 0.900.90, and 0.950.95 at 1.7B, 4B, 8B, and 14B, respectively, but falls to ρ=−0.27\rho=-0.27 at 0.6B. This may reflect insufficiently distinguishable responses at the smallest scale. Within our setting, reliable chat-based model selection therefore emerges only above 0.6B, cautioning against using very small models as proxies for hyperparameter selection. Because the candidate responses and evaluation procedures are held fixed while the judge model changes, this agreement makes it unlikely that the observed coherence is driven solely by idiosyncrasies of a single judge. It does not exclude biases shared across judges or effects of common prompts, aggregation procedures, and comparators. Complete aggregate and benchmark-level correlations appear in Appendix D.3.

4.2 The Hyperparameter Landscape Across Scale

The optimal Qwen3 configuration changes with scale.

Under ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, Figure 4 shows the learning-rate estimates from two-dimensional quadratic response surfaces over (log10⁡LR,log10⁡β)(\log_{10}\mathrm{LR},\log_{10}\beta) at each Qwen3 size. The estimates rise from 0.6B to 1.7B and then decline through 14B, showing an overall downward trend. We use the fitted line only as a descriptive summary of these five Qwen3 models, not as a monotonic scaling law or a predictor for an unseen size. Appendix D.1.3 compares the corresponding estimates under ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}}, ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}}, and validation loss.

The selected configuration changes with the preference dataset.

On Dolci-Instruct-DPO, the best observed ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} configuration uses β=0.01\beta=0.01 at every Qwen3 size. We repeat the shared 3×33\times 3 grid with UltraFeedback at all Qwen3 sizes, retaining the corresponding Dolci-trained SFT checkpoint and evaluation suite. The ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} winners agree at 0.6B, differ only in β\beta at 1.7B, and differ in both coordinates at 4B–14B. Dolci-to-UltraFeedback transfer regret rises from 0.000.00 at 0.6B to 0.250.25 at 1.7B and 0.670.67 at 4B, reaching 1.001.00 at both 8B and 14B, showing that the difference at larger models is consequential. Since β=0.01\beta=0.01 is the lower Dolci boundary and 4×10−64\times 10^{-6} is the upper UltraFeedback boundary, these are preferences within the tested grid rather than located optima. This comparison shows that dataset sensitivity varies across the tested scales; Appendix D.1.12 gives the complete comparison.

4.3 Cheaper Tuning and Transfer

Hyperparameter transfer is unreliable across scales and model families.

The right panel of Figure 4 shows pairwise Spearman correlations between the ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} rankings of the nine configurations shared by every Qwen3 grid. The matrix forms two groups: rankings agree between 0.6B and 1.7B (ρ=0.70\rho=0.70) and among the 4B–14B models (ρ=0.48\rho=0.48–0.820.82), but all correlations across these groups are negative (ρ=−0.72\rho=-0.72 to −0.13-0.13). Transfer also depends on the metric used. Under ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} (Figure 14), the small-model agreement strengthens (ρ=0.93\rho=0.93) and cross-block correlations remain negative (ρ=−0.78\rho=-0.78 to −0.25-0.25), but agreement among the larger models largely disappears (ρ=0.67\rho=0.67 between 4B and 8B, 0.230.23 between 4B and 14B, and −0.02-0.02 between 8B and 14B). Moreover, positive rank agreement does not guarantee low transfer regret. Model-size distance alone is therefore insufficient to determine whether a configuration will transfer. Additional aggregate-specific, transfer, and cross-family analyses appear in Appendix D.5.1–D.5.3.

Partial runs provide an informative but scale-dependent selection signal.

At each Qwen3 size, we compare the intermediate and final ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} rankings over configurations evaluated at both fidelities. After 600 steps (≈30%\approx 30\% of training), their Spearman correlations are 0.850.85, 0.900.90, 0.850.85, 0.760.76, and 0.630.63 from 0.6B to 14B. At 4B, selecting from the step-600 scores yields zero final ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} regret, while directly transferring the configuration selected at 1.7B incurs maximal regret (1.001.00). A short target-model run can therefore provide a more useful selection signal than transfer from a neighbouring scale. Under UltraFeedback, dynamic-ranking correlations at step 144, roughly 30%30\% of training, are 0.850.85, 0.720.72, 0.750.75, 0.670.67, and 0.650.65 from 0.6B to 14B. Because agreement can fluctuate across checkpoints, we use early evaluations to prioritize promising configurations rather than as a universal stopping rule. The complete Qwen3 trajectories on Dolci-Instruct-DPO, UltraFeedback replications, and Llama trajectories are reported in Appendices D.1, D.1.12, and D.2.

Adaptive search methods outperform random search when given sufficient budget.

We compare five search strategies over continuous learning-rate and β\beta domains using four surrogate blackboxes fitted separately to the Qwen3 trajectories: a Gaussian process (GP) and one-, three-, and five-nearest-neighbour (1-NN, 3-NN, and 5-NN) regressors. Each method optimises ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, and we evaluate its recommendation at final fidelity. Under the 8×8\times budget, CQR is the only method with a conclusive improvement over random search under all four surrogates (Table 2). BOHB has the largest GP gain, whereas CQR has the largest gain under each NN surrogate. TPE and BOHB improve conclusively under the GP, 3-NN, and 5-NN surrogates, while ASHA does so under the GP and 3-NN surrogates. Figure 5 shows how GP regret decreases with budget at each model size. The gains are uneven across sizes: separation from random search is largest at 8B and 14B and nearly absent at 1.7B. Thus, the relative advantage of an HPO method depends on the response surface and the model size, although CQR is the most consistent method in these simulations. Under the restrictive budget, no method differs detectably from random search because the budget generally expires before adaptive proposals begin. Complete results and regret curves appear in Appendix D.4.

5 Practical Recommendations

Select configurations using downstream evaluations.

Do not use validation loss alone to choose a DPO configuration: its minimum can be far from the best downstream configuration. Nor should a single downstream benchmark determine the choice, since benchmark rankings often disagree. When the goal is conversational response quality, select using multiple chat benchmarks rather than a single metric, and check individual static benchmarks for regressions. Where two judges yield different configuration rankings, treat the selected configuration as evaluation-dependent and include targeted human assessment before making consequential deployment decisions.

Retune for the target setting.

Treat a configuration from another model or preference dataset as a starting point for a small target-specific search, not as a default. Search learning rate and β\beta jointly: model-size distance does not reliably predict whether configurations retain their ranking, and changing the preference dataset can alter the selected configuration, with substantial transfer regret at larger model sizes. If the selected value lies at the edge of the tested range, extend the range before interpreting it as a well-localized optimum.

Use partial target-model runs before committing full training.

Configuration rankings become informative within 20–30% of training across the model families and preference-data settings studied, making early checkpoints useful for narrowing the candidate set, although they do not guarantee the final winner at every scale. When using adaptive HPO, allocate enough compute for the method to move beyond its initialization phase. Under our larger budget, CQR provides the most consistent improvement, while TPE, ASHA, and BOHB also outperform random search. Because gains vary across model sizes, validate the allocation strategy on the target setting. Our compute budgets include training but exclude evaluations.

6 Limitations

Limited cross-family and preference-data coverage.

The five-size scaling analysis is confined to Qwen3. The three Llama checkpoints span two releases rather than a homogeneous scaling series, so they provide qualitative tests of benchmark agreement and transfer but cannot establish whether the Qwen3 learning-rate trend generalizes across families. We test preference-data sensitivity only on one alternative dataset within one model family, by replacing Dolci-Instruct-DPO with UltraFeedback Binarized while retaining the SFT checkpoint and evaluation suite. One dataset pair cannot establish how common the resulting reversal in preferred learning rate is. The selected Dolci-Instruct learning rates and β\beta values should not be treated as defaults for other datasets.

Finite grids, offline search, and training variance.

We select among logged configurations whose coverage differs across sizes; shared-core transfer need not equal full-grid transfer, and boundary selections need not locate unconstrained optima. The Qwen3-only HPO experiments interpolate logged trajectories through four fitted response surfaces rather than adding DPO runs. Each DPO configuration uses one training seed, and benchmark bootstrapping and 25 HPO seeds measure evaluation-composition and search variation, but not training-seed variance.

Evaluation sensitivity.

At Qwen3-0.6B, the two judges provide conflicting rankings, possibly because small response differences are especially judge-sensitive at this scale. Arena-Hard and MT-Bench also compare configurations with matched SFT checkpoints, which may introduce comparator-specific judge preferences. This limits conclusions from individual metrics or judges.

7 Conclusion

Our findings show that DPO hyperparameter selection depends on the target model, preference data, and evaluation objective. Validation loss can select configurations far from the best-performing downstream configuration, static benchmarks disagree about configuration rankings, and neither parameter-count distance nor a configuration selected on another preference dataset reliably predicts transfer quality. Although the selected Qwen3 learning rate exhibits an overall decline with scale, its small-scale rise and the boundary selection of β\beta argue against a universal configuration or simple transfer rule. Partial target-model runs provide useful ranking information within 2020–30%30\% of training across the model families and training data settings studied, offering a lower-cost way to narrow the candidate set before full training. Continuous-surrogate HPO experiments show that informed search can improve final configuration selection when the 8×8\times budget permits adaptive proposals. The released trajectories provide an offline benchmark for studying this trade-off between selection quality and training cost.

AI use statement

We used generative AI tools to help polish the writing and presentation of this paper. During experimentation, generative AI was used to help prepare Slurm submission scripts and YAML configuration files; all generated files were manually inspected and verified before use. AI was not used to generate the remaining training and HPO simulation code, which was drawn from their respective mentioned libraries. For evaluation and analysis, generative AI was used to help write plotting code that produced figures from the experimental data. We manually checked the resulting plots and their underlying values for correctness. The authors take full responsibility for the paper and for all artifacts produced with AI assistance.

Reproducibility statement

All training and evaluation settings are documented in Section 3 and the Appendix, including the per-size search spaces, optimisation settings, evaluation protocols, and judge configurations. We release a checkpoint-level offline benchmark: https://github.com/HannanJaved/dpo-hpo-blackbox. It contains checkpoint-level evaluation data for all Qwen3 (including the UltraFeedback Binarized replications) and Llama DPO experiments, including training fidelity, elapsed training cost, and scores on the eleven downstream benchmarks. Producing each entry requires a full DPO training run and a costly downstream evaluation suite. The completed DPO runs consumed approximately 8,454 H100 GPU-hours and evaluations (including intermediate checkpoints and two judges) consumed 3,395 H100 GPU-hours; Appendix C.1.1 provides the breakdown and accounting scope of the 11,849 total H100 GPU-hours used. The release enables future work to compare selection signals, early-selection policies, transfer rules, and HPO methods without repeating that compute. The blackbox tables additionally provide ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}}, ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}}, and ZMacroZ_{\mathrm{Macro}} aggregates. The artifact includes manifests, the HPO protocol, and code to reconstruct the Qwen3 blackboxes and surrogate environments. It also provides complete Qwen3 HPO traces across five model sizes, four surrogates, two budgets, three objectives, and five optimisers. The training checkpoints and cluster logs are not included in the artifact due to storage limitations.
