Appendix A Additional Related Work

Hyperparameter optimisation and multi-fidelity search.

Hyperparameter optimisation (HPO) seeks a training configuration that performs well while minimizing the cost of evaluating candidate configurations. In single-fidelity HPO, each candidate is trained to completion before the next informed choice is taken. Bayesian optimisation (BO) instead fits a model to completed trials and uses it to propose new configurations (Franceschi et al., 2025). Multi-fidelity HPO additionally treats partial training runs as cheaper, lower-fidelity evaluations and allocates further training only to candidates that seem promising under the chosen evaluation objective. This is the case in Hyperband, ASHA, and BOHB (Li et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020a; Falkner et al., 2018). We use logged DPO trajectories to compare random search (Bergstra and Bengio, 2012), TPE (Bergstra et al., 2011), CQR (Salinas et al., 2023), ASHA (Li et al., 2020a), and BOHB (Falkner et al., 2018) under matched training-time budgets, treating training progress as fidelity and downstream performance as the objective.

HPO benchmark suites.

Benchmark suites such as HPOBench and YAHPO Gym support controlled, reproducible comparisons of HPO methods on expensive multi-fidelity problems (Eggensperger et al., 2021; Pfisterer et al., 2022). HPOBench packages reproducible benchmark problems, whereas YAHPO Gym uses fitted surrogates to make repeated optimiser comparisons inexpensive. Our released benchmark applies this paradigm to DPO. It provides checkpoint-level trajectories, measured training costs, and downstream evaluation outcomes from expensive post-training runs. It therefore enables future work to compare evaluation signals, early-selection policies, transfer rules, and HPO allocation strategies without repeating the underlying DPO training.

Appendix B Dataset Details

Dataset versions and splits.

Our primary post-training recipe uses the train splits of allenai/Dolci-Instruct-SFT for supervised fine-tuning and allenai/Dolci-Instruct-DPO for preference optimisation (Team Olmo, 2025). The same datasets and preprocessing are used for all Qwen3 and Llama experiments. We split Dolci-Instruct-DPO with test_size=0.005 and seed 42, yielding 258,622 training pairs and a fixed held-out validation set of 1,300 pairs. The Qwen3 preference-data ablations instead use the train_prefs split of HuggingFaceH4/ultrafeedback_binarized (Cui et al., 2024), while retaining the same Dolci-trained SFT checkpoint. Of its 61,135 preference pairs, 60,000 are used for training and 1,135 for validation. Table 3 summarizes the resulting example counts.

SFT formatting and filtering.

SFT examples are represented as messages and formatted with a custom OLMo-style ChatML template using <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> delimiters. The template includes a default system prompt supporting function calling and is saved with each SFT checkpoint as chat_template.jinja. We train with assistant-only loss, masking user and system tokens, and do not use sequence packing. Before training, we discard examples with a missing or invalid messages field or with content=None in any turn, reducing Dolci-Instruct-SFT from 2,152,112 to 1,944,341 examples. We apply no further deduplication or subsampling. The maximum SFT sequence length is 8,192 tokens for all Qwen3 and all Llama models; longer conversations are truncated by SFTTrainer.

DPO formatting and truncation.

The DPO runs load the tokenizer and chat template stored with their corresponding SFT checkpoint. For Dolci-Instruct-DPO, the chosen and rejected conversations are retained while turn-level metadata is removed, leaving only role and content; any existing prompt or messages columns are removed so that TRL reconstructs the common prompt from the two conversations. The same processing is applied to UltraFeedback after retaining only its chosen and rejected columns. Dolci-Instruct-DPO uses a maximum sequence length of 4,096 tokens and a maximum prompt length of 512 tokens. UltraFeedback uses 2,048 and 1,024 tokens, respectively. Both use TRL’s default keep_end truncation mode, which retains the end of an overlength prompt and truncates the response as needed to satisfy the total sequence-length limit. Beyond constructing the validation splits, we apply no additional filtering, deduplication, or subsampling to either DPO dataset.

Appendix C Additional Details On The Experimental Setup

C.1 Training Configurations

Supervised fine-tuning.

We sweep SFT learning rates and use 3×10−53\times 10^{-5} for the SFT checkpoint that initializes every primary DPO run. SFT is run for two epochs, corresponding to approximately 30,382 optimiser steps, with a global batch size of 128. The per-device batch size is one. Most runs use gradient accumulation over 16 steps on eight GPUs; Qwen3-14B uses eight accumulation steps on 16 GPUs, preserving the same global batch size. We optimise with adamw_torch, Adam coefficients (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.999)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999), ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, no weight decay, and maximum gradient norm 1.0. The learning rate follows a linear schedule with a 0.03 warmup ratio. Training uses bfloat16 precision and seed 42. Checkpoints are saved every 3,000 steps for Qwen3 and Llama models.

Direct preference optimisation.

The primary DPO grids vary learning rate and β\beta while holding the remaining settings fixed. Each configuration is trained for one epoch, with the logged trajectories ending at approximately 2,031 optimiser steps. We use a per-device batch size of one on eight GPUs and 16 gradient-accumulation steps, giving a global batch size of 128. The optimiser is adamw_torch with the same Adam coefficients, numerical stability constant, zero weight decay, and maximum gradient norm as SFT. We use a linear learning-rate schedule with a 0.1 warmup ratio, bfloat16 precision, seed 8, the standard sigmoid DPO loss, and zero label smoothing. Checkpoints are saved every 200 steps, and the final checkpoint is also evaluated. Downstream evaluations are run separately on these saved checkpoints.

The Qwen3 UltraFeedback experiments use the same DPO recipe, except for the sequence-length settings reported in Appendix B and 32 gradient-accumulation steps. With four GPUs, this gives a global batch size of 128. Its one-epoch runs contain approximately 469 optimiser steps; for the trajectory analysis, we evaluate checkpoints every 48 steps and the final checkpoint.

Hardware and distributed training.

All training runs use NVIDIA H100 GPUs and are executed through Slurm with four GPUs per node. Table 6 reports the number of GPUs and distributed strategy used for each model group. The primary Dolci-Instruct DPO runs use eight GPUs, the UltraFeedback ablation uses four, and the largest SFT run, Qwen3-14B, uses 16 GPUs.

C.1.1 Compute Accounting

We estimate compute as the number of allocated NVIDIA H100 GPUs multiplied by job wall-clock time. Table 5 reports training and benchmark-evaluation compute for the model and preference-data combinations analysed in this paper. Each distinct evaluation is counted once; when an evaluation was resubmitted, we retain only the latest completed job. Evaluation compute includes LM Evaluation Harness tasks, response generation, AlpacaEval, LLM-judge scoring, and Elo estimation at final and intermediate checkpoints. Distinct evaluations account for approximately 29% of the reported training-and-evaluation workload. Jobs that were cancelled/crashed mid-run, SFT runs, and offline HPO simulation are excluded.

C.2 SFT Learning-Rate Sweep

We evaluate SFT learning rates ∈{10−6,10−5,3×10−5,5×10−5,5×10−4}\in\{10^{-6},10^{-5},3\times 10^{-5},5\times 10^{-5},5\times 10^{-4}\} for each Qwen3 model size. Scores are standardized separately within each model size and evaluation aggregate. No single moderate learning rate value dominates across all sizes or across our aggregates (ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}}, ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}}, ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}), with the relative rankings varying with both scale and objective. We therefore hold the SFT learning rate fixed at 3×10−53\times 10^{-5} in the primary DPO experiments, rather than selecting a separate SFT optimum per size, which would confound cross-size DPO comparisons. The sweep serves as a sensitivity check that this choice lies in the non-degenerate plateau rather than as a claim that 3×10−53\times 10^{-5} is uniquely optimal. By contrast, 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} consistently yields substantially worse downstream scores, especially on ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} (Figure 6).

C.3 Search Spaces per Model Scale

Every primary grid contains the nine configurations in the shared core

{1,2,4}×10−6​(learning rate)×{0.01,0.02,0.04}​(β).\{1,2,4\}\!\times\!10^{-6}\ \text{(learning rate)}\quad\times\quad\{0.01,0.02,0.04\}\ \text{($\beta$)}.

This common core enables like-for-like transfer comparisons across Qwen3 sizes and between Qwen3 and Llama. We extend the grid at individual Qwen3 sizes to cover the locally promising learning-rate range and, at 4B, an additional β\beta value. Table 7 gives the exact configurations. Cross-scale and cross-family transfer are evaluated on the shared core, whereas full-grid optima and response-surface analyses use every available configuration at the corresponding size.

Beyond the shared core, Qwen3-4B adds β=0.08\beta=0.08 at learning rates 11, 22, and 4×10−64\times 10^{-6}; all four tested β\beta values at 8×10−68\times 10^{-6}; and (4×10−7,0.01)(4\times 10^{-7},0.01) and (8×10−7,0.01)(8\times 10^{-7},0.01). Qwen3-14B adds (4×10−7,β)(4\times 10^{-7},\beta) and (8×10−7,β)(8\times 10^{-7},\beta) for β∈{0.01,0.02,0.04}\beta\in\{0.01,0.02,0.04\}, plus (1×10−7,0.01)(1\times 10^{-7},0.01) and (8×10−8,0.01)(8\times 10^{-8},0.01).

For the Dolci-Instruct grids, we evaluate checkpoints every 200 steps and at the final training step. For UltraFeedback, we evaluate checkpoints every 48 steps and at the final step. These intervals correspond to evaluations at approximately 10%10\% intervals of training progress for both datasets. These trajectories support the early-selection and offline HPO analyses. The validation loss directed Bayesian-optimisation sweeps use continuous learning-rate and β\beta domains and are described separately in Appendix E.

C.4 Evaluation Benchmark Settings

C.4.1 Static Benchmarks

We evaluate static tasks with lm-evaluation-harness. Model weights are loaded in bfloat16 precision, and log-likelihood tasks use scaled dot-product attention. Table 8 reports the splits, sample counts, few-shot settings, and metrics; inference details are given immediately below it. Except for IFEval, these tasks are evaluated as raw-text completions without applying the model’s chat template, matching their standard harness protocols and facilitating comparison with previously reported results.

ARC-C, GPQA-Diamond, HellaSwag, PIQA, and TruthfulQA-MC2 are scored by comparing the likelihood of the answer choices; normalised accuracy is used where shown in Table 8. GSM8K uses greedy generation with a limit of 1,024 new tokens and its standard stop strings. IFEval also uses greedy generation, with a limit of 1,280 new tokens, and averages prompt- and instruction-level accuracy under both strict and loose matching. GPQA and IFEval use the only splits supplied by their source datasets. TruthfulQA’s nominal zero-shot setting includes the fixed six-example QA preamble embedded in its standard prompt.

IFEval chat-template convention.

The default IFEval scores apply the chat template stored with each model. These scores are used in the heatmaps, aggregate trajectories, benchmark correlations, and phase-gain analyses.

C.4.2 Chat-based evaluations

We evaluate every chat benchmark independently with two judges: Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 and Gemma 4 31B-it. Both judges evaluate the same generated candidate and comparator responses using identical prompts, decoding settings, response-order rules, tie handling, and aggregation procedures; only the judge model changes. This controlled comparison isolates sensitivity to judge choice. Table 9 summarizes the comparator and reported score for each benchmark; response-order and aggregation details follow the table.

Arena-Hard judges every comparison in both response orders; ties contribute 0.5, and strong preferences receive threefold weight in the bootstrap. MT-Bench uses a fixed order with the candidate first and the SFT comparator second; ties again contribute 0.5. Its reference-assisted prompts are used for relevant mathematics, reasoning, and coding questions. AlpacaEval randomizes response order deterministically for each instruction and computes a continuous preference from the two possible one-token judgments. Elo evaluates each comparison in both orders and fits a Bradley–Terry model to the resulting pairwise scores; exact ties and unparseable judgments contribute 0.5 to each response.

Table 10 gives the decoding settings for candidate-response generation and both judges. Arena-Hard and AlpacaEval generate candidate responses greedily. MT-Bench follows the FastChat category-specific temperatures. Elo is the only pipeline that samples both candidate and judge outputs: submitted jobs inherit the JudgeArena ChatVLLM defaults of temperature 0.6 and top_p=0.95\texttt{top\_p}=0.95. Consequently, individual Elo evaluations are stochastic across repeated executions, unlike the other three pipelines under the submitted settings.

For MT-Bench, candidate-generation temperatures are kept at their default values: 0.7 for writing and role-playing, 0.1 for STEM and humanities, and 0 for extraction, mathematics, coding, reasoning, and Arena-Hard-200 categories. We use the reference prompt templates supplied by Arena-Hard v2.0, MT-Bench, and AlpacaEval 2.0.

C.4.3 Held-out DPO loss

For the primary Dolci-Instruct grids, we construct the fixed 1,300-pair validation set described in Appendix B. We do not evaluate on this set during DPO training. After training, we evaluate the latest saved checkpoint, or the final model when no intermediate checkpoint is available, once on the held-out pairs. The resulting loss is the validation loss value used in Section 4.1. The validation loss directed Bayesian-optimisation experiments use the same held-out set but evaluate loss every 100 training steps and save checkpoints every 400 steps.

C.5 Hyperparameter-optimisation Simulation Settings

Compared optimisers.

We compare three single-fidelity methods, which train each proposed configuration to completion, with two methods that use intermediate training results to allocate further compute:

  • •

    Random search samples learning-rate and β\beta configurations independently of previous outcomes (Bergstra and Bengio, 2012).

  • •

    TPE models regions associated with good and poor completed trials using separate density estimators, then proposes configurations favoured by their density ratio (Bergstra et al., 2011).

  • •

    CQR fits conformalized quantile-regression models to predict performance and uncertainty from completed configurations, then uses these estimates to propose subsequent configurations (Salinas et al., 2023).

  • •

    ASHA uses asynchronous successive halving: candidates with strong partial-training results receive more training, while weaker candidates are stopped at intermediate resource levels (Li et al., 2020a).

  • •

    BOHB combines model-based configuration proposals with Hyperband-style allocation of training resources across candidates (Falkner et al., 2018).

Simulation protocol and compute budgets.

Each simulation searches a continuous domain in (log10⁡LR,log10⁡β)(\log_{10}\mathrm{LR},\log_{10}\beta) bounded by the minimum and maximum values measured at that model size. Training progress is the fidelity variable, with checkpoints at steps 200, 400, …\ldots, 2,000 and the final step 2,031; the surrogate’s cumulative training time is the trial cost. Two trials run in parallel, and each optimiser–surrogate–size setting is repeated with 25 random seeds. We define one budget unit as the measured wall-clock duration of one complete reference DPO run. The larger budget is eight units, which allows CQR’s five initial random trials to finish and leaves time for adaptive proposals. The restrictive budget is one unit, corresponding to approximately two full-run equivalents of total compute across both workers.

We compare random search, the tree-structured Parzen estimator (TPE), conformalized quantile regression (CQR), asynchronous successive halving (ASHA), and Bayesian optimisation with Hyperband (BOHB). For TPE, we set top_n_percent=33 and num_min_data_points=3; all other TPE settings use the implementation defaults. Random search, TPE, and CQR evaluate configurations to completion, whereas ASHA and BOHB may terminate candidates at intermediate checkpoints. All methods receive the same time limit, workers, and continuous domain. ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} is the primary maximization objective; ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} is retained as a cross-objective evaluation.

Successive-halving schedules.

ASHA and BOHB use a single successive-halving bracket with a grace period of 400 steps and reduction factor two, yielding comparisons at steps 400, 800, and 1,600 before final fidelity. Approximately half of the active configurations are retained at each comparison. Delaying the first decision until step 400 avoids pruning at step 200, where the 8B and 14B ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} rankings are poorly aligned with their final orderings.

Continuous surrogate environments.

The logged grids answer only at observed configurations, so we construct continuous surrogate versions of every per-size benchmark. Learning rate and β\beta are transformed to base-10 logarithms, and no query extrapolates outside the measured range. Training step remains discrete, and one fitted model predicts the complete trajectory at the recorded fidelities.

We fit four alternatives separately and never pool their predictions: one-nearest-neighbour regression, which is piecewise constant between measured configurations; distance-weighted three- and five-nearest-neighbour regression; and a Gaussian process with a constant component, Matérn-5/25/2 kernel, and white-noise term initialized to 10−210^{-2}. GP targets are normalised, kernel optimisation uses three restarts, and the fitting seed is zero. These environments test sensitivity to different interpolation assumptions and do not constitute additional observed DPO runs.

Recommendation and scoring.

At a budget cutoff, we recommend the trial with the highest search score at final step 2,031 whenever at least one trial has completed. If no trial has completed, we compare only trials evaluated at the highest fidelity shared within that run. We then evaluate the recommended (LR,β)(\mathrm{LR},\beta) at true final fidelity on the same surrogate. This prevents an optimiser from benefiting merely because it reports more intermediate checkpoints. For pooled comparisons, we first average the five model-size outcomes within each seed and then form a 95% tt-interval across the 25 seed-level averages. Differences from random search are paired by seed.

Appendix D Additional Experimental Results

D.1 Qwen3 Experiments

D.1.1 Benchmark-Level Agreement And Validation Loss

Figure 7 gives the complete benchmark-level rank-correlation matrices underlying the aggregate analyses in Section 4.1. Each matrix shows that the relationship between negative validation loss and downstream rankings varies across both benchmarks and model sizes. It can align positively with some evaluations while being weakly or negatively associated with others, explaining why validation loss does not provide a reliable aggregate selection signal.

D.1.2 Validation signals at fixed β\beta

DPO loss changes with β\beta, so its values need not be directly comparable across the full grid. As a sensitivity check, we rank learning rates by lower final validation loss and higher final ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} separately within each β\beta, then pool those within-β\beta ranks to compute Spearman correlation. From Qwen3-0.6B through 14B, the resulting correlations are −0.67-0.67, 0.330.33, 0.050.05, 0.300.30, and 0.670.67. The corresponding full-grid correlations are −0.48-0.48, 0.370.37, 0.150.15, 0.120.12, and 0.050.05. Fixed-β\beta comparisons therefore do not produce consistently strong agreement with downstream performance, although the relationship varies substantially by size.

We also compare TRL training reward accuracy with ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}}. Unlike the magnitude of the DPO loss, the chosen-versus-rejected decision is unchanged by multiplying a fixed policy’s reward margin by positive β\beta. Its within-β\beta correlations are 0.950.95, 1.001.00, −0.23-0.23, −0.40-0.40, and 0.110.11 across the same sizes. Reward accuracy is informative at the two smallest Qwen3 sizes but does not consistently rank configurations at larger sizes. Each β\beta slice contains only a few learning rates, so these correlations describe the tested configurations rather than precise population relationships.

D.1.3 Objective-Specific Learning-Rate Trends

The learning-rate trend in Section 4.2 uses ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, but the descriptive relationship depends on the evaluation objective. Figure 9 compares the corresponding learning-rate estimates for ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}}, ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}}, ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, and validation loss. At each Qwen3 size, we fit a two-dimensional quadratic response surface over (log10⁡LR,log10⁡β)(\log_{10}\mathrm{LR},\log_{10}\beta) and extract its preferred learning rate.

The estimates differ across selection signals, particularly at larger sizes: ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}} favours higher learning rates than ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, while validation loss follows a different pattern again. These response-surface estimates summarize preferences within the measured grids; they are neither unconstrained optima nor predictions for an unseen model size.

D.1.4 Final aggregate optima

Table 11 reports the best observed final configuration under each evaluation aggregate. The ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} selections reproduce the non-monotonic pattern discussed in Section 4.2: the learning rate first rises from 0.6B to 1.7B and then decreases through 14B. The objective-specific columns show that this pattern should not be separated from the evaluation criterion. At 8B, for example, ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} selects a learning rate of 4×10−74\times 10^{-7} whereas ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}} selects 4×10−64\times 10^{-6}. The selected β\beta also differs across objectives at 0.6B, 1.7B, and 14B.

D.1.5 Dynamic–static trade-offs across Qwen3 sizes

Figure 11 extends the Qwen3-4B comparison in Figure 3 to the remaining model sizes. At each size, the configurations maximizing ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} and ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}} occupy different locations on, or near, the Pareto frontier. Thus, the objective-specific learning-rate choices in Table 11 reflect a dynamic–static trade-off across the Qwen3 family rather than only the 4B grid.

D.1.6 ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} response surfaces

Figure 12 shows the final ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} response surface over the configurations evaluated at each Qwen3 size. The preferred region shifts toward lower learning rates at larger sizes, while the irregular and size-specific surface shapes reinforce that a configuration selected at one scale need not rank well at another. Blank cells denote configurations that were not evaluated at that size.

D.1.7 Equal-group aggregate robustness

ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} weights each benchmark equally, which assigns seven of eleven total weights to the static group. We therefore define

ZMacro=12​(ZDynamic+ZStatic),Z_{\mathrm{Macro}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(Z_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}+Z_{\mathrm{Static}}\right),

giving chat and static benchmarks equal total weight. The ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} and ZMacroZ_{\mathrm{Macro}} configuration rankings remain highly correlated at every Qwen3 size (ρ=0.903\rho=0.903–0.9940.994). Their selected configurations match at 0.6B, 1.7B, and 14B, while the preferred learning rate differs at 4B and 8B. Thus, equal group weighting can alter the precise selected configuration, but it preserves the main conclusions about validation loss and cross-scale ranking instability.

Minimum-validation-loss selection remains unreliable under ZMacroZ_{\mathrm{Macro}}: its mean normalised regret is 0.570.57, and the combined Spearman correlation between negative validation loss and ZMacroZ_{\mathrm{Macro}} is only 0.160.16. Cross-scale agreement also remains non-monotonic in model-size distance (Figure 14).

D.1.8 Stability of the selected configuration

We ask whether the selected configuration depends heavily on the particular benchmarks included in an aggregate. For each aggregate, we repeatedly resample its constituent benchmarks with replacement, recompute configuration scores on the shared 3×33\times 3 core, and record whether the winner from the original aggregate remains selected. Figure 15 reports this recovery probability. All three aggregates recover their original winner more often than the 1/91/9 uniform reference, but stability differs by objective. ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} recovers its winner in 52.052.0–93.7%93.7\% of resamples and is more stable than ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}} at every Qwen3 size. ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} recovers its winner in 48.348.3–70.6%70.6\% of resamples. This analysis measures sensitivity to benchmark composition only and not the uncertainty within an individual benchmark.

D.1.9 Benchmark-pair agreement

Figure 16 expands the group summaries in Table 1 into their constituent benchmark pairs. Every chat-benchmark pair is positively correlated at every model size, although the strength of agreement varies. Static-benchmark pairs span strong positive and negative correlations at the same size. Their low mean agreement therefore reflects conflicting configuration rankings across capabilities rather than uniformly uninformative benchmarks.

D.1.10 Ranking stability during training

Figure 17 reports the complete ranking-stability trajectories underlying the step-600 values in Section 4.3. For this longitudinal comparison, each benchmark is standardized using the mean and population standard deviation of its final scores across the corresponding model-size grid; the same transformation is then applied to every intermediate checkpoint. This keeps the benchmark scale fixed over training. At each step, we compute the Spearman correlation between the intermediate and final configuration rankings using configurations observed at both points.

The trajectories confirm that useful ranking information appears early but at different rates across scales and objectives. At step 600, ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} correlations are 0.850.85, 0.900.90, 0.850.85, 0.760.76, and 0.630.63 from 0.6B through 14B. The 1.7B ranking is already highly stable at the first checkpoint, while 14B improves more gradually. Several trajectories fluctuate after becoming informative, which is why we use early scores to allocate additional training rather than prescribe one universal stopping checkpoint.

D.1.11 Early-selection regret

Rank correlation measures the full ordering, whereas configuration selection depends mainly on the top of that ordering. Figure 18 therefore evaluates the final regret of the configuration that would be selected at each checkpoint. For this cross-sectional calculation, benchmark means and standard deviations are recomputed separately at every checkpoint over the configurations available at that exact step. We then select the highest-scoring ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} configuration and measure its final ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} regret relative to the best and worst final configurations in that model-size grid.

Low or zero regret can be reached well before exhaustive training, but the best selection checkpoint is not monotonic or shared across sizes. This variability motivates multi-fidelity allocation rather than a fixed early-stopping rule.

D.1.12 UltraFeedback preference-data ablation

We repeat the shared nine-configuration DPO grid on UltraFeedback at all five Qwen3 model sizes. These experiments retain the corresponding Dolci-trained SFT checkpoint, DPO objective, and evaluation suite, while using UltraFeedback and its dataset-specific sequence-length settings. Table 12 compares the ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} winners on the common grid and measures the regret from transferring each dataset’s selected configuration to the other dataset.

The shared-grid winners agree at 0.6B, differ only in β\beta at 1.7B, and differ in both learning rate and β\beta at 4B–14B. Cross-dataset regret follows the same pattern: it is zero at 0.6B, limited at 1.7B, and substantial at 4B–14B. This five-size comparison strengthens the evidence for preference-data sensitivity, but does not establish a general scaling relationship. Moreover, every UltraFeedback ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} winner uses the upper learning-rate boundary, 4×10−64\times 10^{-6}; the 1.7B–14B winners also use the upper tested β\beta. These results therefore identify preferences within the shared grid.

At 0.6B, ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}} varies over a much narrower range than ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, making its particular argmax less informative. The stronger and more consistent UltraFeedback result is that ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} and ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} both favour the upper tested learning rates at all sizes.

Figure 19 compares intermediate and final rankings across the five UltraFeedback sizes. Dynamic-evaluation rankings are generally informative by 144 steps, roughly 30%30\% of training: correlations are at least 0.650.65 for all sizes. The 1.7B dynamic ranking is a useful counterexample to a fixed earlier cutoff, falling to 0.080.08 at step 96 before recovering at step 144. These results support using early target-model evaluations to prioritize candidates, while reinforcing that a fixed early-stopping point is not reliable across objectives or model sizes.

Benchmark agreement under UltraFeedback.

The qualitative difference between dynamic and static benchmark agreement also holds under UltraFeedback. Across all tested sizes, dynamic benchmarks produce higher mean pairwise configuration-ranking correlations than static benchmarks (Table 13). Thus, the greater consistency of chat-based evaluations is not specific to the Dolci-Instruct-DPO preference data.

D.2 Llama Experiments

We repeat the principal analyses on Llama 3.2 at 1B and 3B parameters and on Llama 3.1 at 8B, using the same Dolci-Instruct SFT and preference data, training objective, nine-configuration core, and evaluation suite as in the Qwen3 experiments. Because the 8B model belongs to a different Llama release, we use it as a complementary transfer test rather than treating the three sizes as observations from one scaling series.

D.2.1 Final aggregate optima

Table 14 reports the best observed final configuration under each aggregate. Under ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}}, the selected learning rate rises from 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} at Llama 3.2-1B to 4×10−64\times 10^{-6} at Llama 3.2-3B, matching the small-scale rise observed for Qwen3. We do not fit a Llama learning-rate scaling law, since the 8B experiment changes both model size and model version. The differences across columns also reinforce that an “optimal” DPO configuration is conditional on the evaluation objective: ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} and ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}} select different learning rates at every Llama size.

D.2.2 Benchmark agreement and sensitivity to AlpacaEval

Table 15 gives the mean and population standard deviation of pairwise benchmark-ranking correlations. Using all four chat benchmarks, chat agreement exceeds static agreement at 1B and 3B. At 8B, however, AlpacaEval ranks the configurations differently from the other three chat evaluations: the mean chat correlation is 0.320.32 with a standard deviation of 0.610.61. Excluding AlpacaEval in a sensitivity analysis raises the 8B chat mean to 0.920.92 and reduces its standard deviation to 0.040.04. The same exclusion has much smaller effects at 1B and 3B. This does not determine which evaluation is correct, but it shows that an aggregate can conceal disagreement specific to one benchmark and model setting. The selected 8B ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} and ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} configurations are unchanged by this exclusion, even though the agreement statistics change substantially. One plausible contributor is the evaluation mechanism: AlpacaEval is the only chat evaluation in our study implemented as a one-token pairwise classifier, with its preference recovered from the relative probabilities of two label tokens and no generated rationale. This protocol difference may make its rankings more sensitive to prompt or calibration effects. However, our comparison does not isolate this mechanism from other differences in prompts, reference responses, or aggregation, so we treat it solely as our hypothesis.

Table 16 reports the individual chat-benchmark pairs behind these summaries. The three comparisons that do not involve AlpacaEval remain strongly positive at 8B, while all three comparisons involving AlpacaEval are negative. At 1B and 3B, every chat pair is positively correlated.

D.2.3 Ranking stability and early selection

Figure 20 applies the fixed-final normalization described in Appendix D.1: each benchmark’s final-grid mean and population standard deviation are used to transform every checkpoint before comparing intermediate and final rankings. Llama 3.2-1B and 3B develop high ranking correlations early in training. The Llama 3.1-8B ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} trajectory is less stable and changes markedly when AlpacaEval is excluded, consistent with the pairwise disagreement above. This sensitivity concerns the ordering of the full grid; the final ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}}-selected configuration remains (4×10−6,0.02)(4\times 10^{-6},0.02) in both variants.

Figure 21 measures the top-of-ranking decision directly, using the per-checkpoint standardization defined for Figure 18. At step 400, approximately 20%20\% of a full run, early ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} selection identifies the eventual best configuration at 3B and 8B and incurs normalised regret of 0.1450.145 at 1B. The 1B optimum is first selected at step 1,400, and its selected configuration fluctuates again at the final intermediate checkpoint. Thus, the Llama results confirm that partial target-model runs can sharply reduce tuning cost, while also showing why a fixed stopping point cannot guarantee the best configuration at every scale.

D.3 Judge Agreement Across Chat Evaluations

We compare configuration rankings rather than raw scores because the two judges need not use the same numerical scale. For each model size and chat benchmark, we restrict the comparison to configurations evaluated by both Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct and Gemma 4 31B-it and compute their Spearman rank correlation. To compare the aggregate rankings, we standardize each judge’s scores separately within the common configuration pool, average the four resulting benchmark z-scores into ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, and correlate the two ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} rankings.

Table 17 reports the complete results. Aggregate agreement is high from 1.7B onward, with ρ\rho between 0.900.90 and 0.980.98, and is 0.790.79 when all 52 jointly evaluated configurations are pooled. Agreement is not uniformly high at the benchmark level: for example, MT-Bench has ρ=0.45\rho=0.45 at 14B and Elo has ρ=0.57\rho=0.57 at 8B. Nevertheless, their aggregate rankings remain strongly correlated, suggesting that averaging several chat evaluations reduces sensitivity to judge-specific differences on an individual benchmark.

The 0.6B grid is the clear exception. Its ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} rankings are negatively correlated (ρ=−0.27\rho=-0.27), driven particularly by Elo (ρ=−0.73\rho=-0.73) and, more weakly, MT-Bench (ρ=−0.17\rho=-0.17). The practical effect is also visible near the top of the ranking: among the five configurations preferred by each judge, the overlap is only one for Elo and two for MT-Bench, compared with three for Arena-Hard and AlpacaEval. At 4B, by contrast, the judges share four of their top five Arena-Hard configurations and all five for each of the other chat benchmarks. These comparisons support using a second judge for consequential decisions at the smallest scale, while also showing that high aggregate agreement does not imply identical judgments on every constituent benchmark.

D.4 Continuous-Surrogate HPO Results

Table 18 reports the end-of-budget comparison. Every method searches ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, recommendations are selected using the common-fidelity rule in Appendix C.5, and each recommendation is scored at final fidelity. Under the 8×8\times wall-clock budget, CQR is the only method with a paired 95% interval excluding zero for every surrogate. BOHB has the largest mean improvement under the Gaussian-process surrogate (0.0980.098), whereas CQR has the largest improvement under the 1-NN, 3-NN, and 5-NN environments (0.090.09, 0.110.11, and 0.160.16). TPE improves conclusively under the GP, 3-NN, and 5-NN surrogates; ASHA does so under the GP and 3-NN environments.

The pooled GP result is heterogeneous across sizes. Table 19 shows that CQR improves conclusively at 0.6B, 4B, and 8B, with its largest gain at 8B (0.200.20). At 14B, ASHA and BOHB have the largest conclusive gains (0.290.29 and 0.240.24), whereas CQR is inconclusive. At 1.7B, none of the informed methods has a conclusive advantage. These differences reinforce the need to validate the search strategy on the target setting rather than infer its value from a single scale.

Under the restrictive one-unit budget, all five methods have statistically indistinguishable pooled ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} scores for every surrogate. This budget permits only approximately two full-run equivalents across both workers and generally expires before the methods can move beyond their common initialization. We therefore treat it as evidence that adaptive search requires an initialization budget, rather than as a comparison of the optimisers themselves.

Figures 22–25 show recommendation quality throughout the larger-budget runs. The larger budget is labelled “generous” inside these figures. These curves use only the configuration recommended at each cutoff and score it at final fidelity; they do not use the maximum checkpoint score observed so far. The curves show that relative ordering can differ by surrogate and can change when the ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}-selected recommendation is evaluated on ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}}. Per-size recommendation curves for every surrogate are included in the released artifact; Table 19 provides the corresponding compact GP summary.

These simulations interpolate the logged runs rather than adding new DPO observations. Agreement across the four independently fitted response surfaces makes the optimiser comparison less dependent on one interpolation scheme, but it does not remove uncertainty between measured configurations. We therefore interpret the results as evidence about search behaviour on the released offline benchmark, not as additional evidence about the exact location of the DPO optimum.

D.5 Transferring Hyperparameters

D.5.1 Cross-scale ranking agreement by evaluation aggregate

The main paper reports cross-scale ranking agreement under ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}. Figure 26 compares it with the static-benchmark ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}} aggregates. The same lack of a simple size-based transfer pattern remains under both aggregates. Under ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, the two smallest models agree positively, as do the 4B, 8B, and 14B models, but rankings reverse between these groups. Under ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}}, agreement is more heterogeneous and several adjacent model pairs have weak or negative correlation. Thus, the instability of configuration rankings across scale is not specific to the chat-benchmark aggregate.

D.5.2 Directed cross-scale transfer

We evaluate direct transfer on the nine configurations shared by all five Qwen3 grids. For each source size, we select its best final ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} configuration within this common set and evaluate that exact configuration at every target size. Normalised regret is computed relative to the target’s best and worst configurations in the same shared set. Restricting both selection and evaluation to this common support avoids treating an unobserved target configuration as transferable. It also means that the 1.7B source uses its core-restricted optimum, (4×10−6,0.01)(4\times 10^{-6},0.01), rather than its full-grid optimum at learning rate 8×10−68\times 10^{-6}.

Figure 27 gives both the smaller-to-larger transfers and the complete directed matrix. Model-size distance is not predictive: 0.6B→\rightarrow1.7B has zero regret, while 1.7B→\rightarrow4B has regret 0.9970.997 despite being a smaller scale change; 0.6B→\rightarrow8B has regret only 0.2870.287. Transfer is also asymmetric. The configuration selected at 8B incurs regret 0.0280.028 at 4B, whereas the 4B selection incurs regret 0.2220.222 at 8B. Similarly, 4B→\rightarrow14B has regret 0.7840.784, compared with 0.2510.251 in the reverse direction. These results rule out parameter-count distance as a sufficient criterion for deciding whether a configuration should be reused.

D.5.3 Cross-family

We next compare ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} rankings over the same nine configurations between the nearest available Qwen3 and Llama sizes. Scores are standardized separately within each model’s grid, so the analysis compares configuration orderings rather than absolute score levels. Figure 28 shows positive agreement for Qwen3-0.6B and Llama 3.2-1B (ρ=0.67\rho=0.67), but negative agreement for Qwen3-4B and Llama 3.2-3B (ρ=−0.67\rho=-0.67) and for Qwen3-8B and Llama 3.1-8B (ρ=−0.40\rho=-0.40). Similar parameter counts therefore do not ensure that the two families prefer the same DPO configuration.

This comparison is exploratory. It contains only three model pairs, two pairs are not exactly size-matched, and the 8B comparison uses Llama 3.1 whereas the smaller Llama models use Llama 3.2. The results establish that cross-family ranking reversal occurs in the tested settings, but they do not estimate how frequently it should occur across model families.

Appendix E Preliminary Validation Loss Directed BO Runs

Before constructing the primary grids, we ran a separate sequential search over DPO learning rate and β\beta at each Qwen3 size, using held-out DPO loss as the objective. These experiments train every proposed configuration and are distinct from the offline HPO simulations in Section 4.3: here, BO chooses continuous hyperparameters by minimizing validation loss, whereas the offline experiments compare search algorithms using downstream evaluation aggregates. The runs also start from SFT checkpoints trained with full-sequence loss, rather than the assistant-only-loss checkpoints used by the primary grids. We therefore report them as preliminary evidence and do not pool their configurations with the main analyses.

Search protocol.

We use Optuna’s tree-structured Parzen estimator (TPE) (Akiba et al., 2019; Bergstra et al., 2011). TPE fits separate Parzen density models to configurations with relatively low and high observed loss and proposes points using its expected-improvement density ratio. Each model-size study begins with five startup trials, then continues sequentially to a fixed budget of 20 trials. No pruning or improvement-based stopping rule is used. The objective is the DPO loss on the same fixed 1,300-pair validation set used in Section 4.1; it is evaluated every 100 training steps. Table 20 gives the remaining search settings.

Validation loss remains unreliable for chat-based selection.

Table 21 evaluates the completed trial with the lowest validation loss at each size. Of the 100 proposed trials, 93 have both validation loss and all three downstream aggregates in the export; trials missing either quantity are excluded. Regret is normalised within the complete preliminary trials for that model, with zero denoting the best downstream score and one the worst. The selected learning rate rises from 0.6B to 1.7B and then decreases from 4.69×10−54.69\times 10^{-5} at 1.7B to 4.38×10−64.38\times 10^{-6} at 14B, a 10.7×10.7\times reduction that resembles the non-monotonic shape observed in the primary grids. The selected β\beta has no monotonic size trend but remains in the lower part of its search domain: it is 0.0110.011–0.0640.064 from 1.7B to 14B, while the 0.6B selection, 0.0530.053, is close to that run’s lower bound of 0.050.05. We therefore interpret the preliminary runs as additional evidence that larger models above 1.7B favour lower learning rates under this training recipe, while supporting only the weaker conclusion that the preferred β\beta remains low rather than constant across scale.

The downstream quality of the minimum-loss trial depends strongly on the evaluation objective. Mean regret across sizes is 0.210.21 for ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}} and 0.160.16 for ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}}, but 0.390.39 for ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}. At 1.7B, the minimum-loss trial ranks 16th of 18 under ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}} and incurs 0.890.89 regret; at 4B, it ranks 16th of 19 with 0.480.48 regret. Conversely, it is optimal under ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}} at 4B and 14B. Thus, adaptive sampling does not make validation loss a uniformly reliable downstream objective: in these runs it aligns more closely with static performance than with chat-based performance.

Rank correlations give the same qualification. We compute Spearman correlation between negative validation loss, so that larger values are better, and each downstream aggregate. Averaged across sizes, the correlations are 0.540.54 with ZAllZ_{\mathrm{All}}, 0.160.16 with ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, and 0.670.67 with ZStaticZ_{\mathrm{Static}}. For ZDynamicZ_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}, the correlation is negative at 1.7B (−0.45-0.45) and 4B (−0.20-0.20), showing that lower validation loss can favour the opposite configuration ordering from chat-based evaluation. Because these searches use a different SFT loss, search domain, and adaptively sampled set of configurations, their absolute regrets are not directly comparable to those of the primary grids in Section 4.1.

Benchmark agreement persists on the adaptively sampled configurations.

Although TPE queries a different, continuous set of configurations at each size, the qualitative agreement pattern from Section 4.1 remains visible. Table 22 reports the mean and population standard deviation of the pairwise Spearman correlations within each evaluation group. Mean chat-benchmark agreement is positive at every size and increases from 0.490.49 at 0.6B to 0.850.85 at 14B. Static agreement is lower throughout, ranging from 0.080.08 to 0.360.36, with substantially larger variation across benchmark pairs. Because IFEval was not available for enough preliminary trials to estimate its pairwise correlations, the static summary uses the other six static benchmarks. At 8B, the chat summary uses the three available pairs among Arena-Hard, MT-Bench, and Elo; the other sizes use all six chat-benchmark pairs. Pairwise correlations are computed over the configurations for which both constituent evaluations are available, yielding 16–20 configurations depending on model size and benchmark pair.

Together, these results show that the contrast between chat and static rankings is not confined to the rectangular grids. They also explain why a validation loss directed search can appear successful under some static evaluations while selecting a poor chat configuration: the two evaluation groups induce different configuration rankings, and validation loss aligns much more strongly with the static group in this preliminary training recipe.
